Ha detto che sarebbe arrivata il giorno dopo

You report in the past what someone said: you change the tenses (è → era, verrà → sarebbe venuto), the persons and the time and place markers (domani → il giorno dopo, qui → lì), and you transform orders and questions.
She said she would arrive the next day.
She asked me if I had already booked the restaurant.
She urged us not to tell her husband anything.
He said that he was tired that day.
She told me it was cold there.
To go from direct to reported speech with the introducing verb in the past: ha detto che…
To change the tenses: present → imperfetto, passato prossimo → trapassato, future → condizionale passato.
To change the markers: oggi → quel giorno, ieri → il giorno prima, domani → il giorno dopo, qui → lì, questo → quello.
To change the persons: «Io vengo» → ha detto che lui veniva.
To turn the imperative into di + infinitive: «Non dire niente!» → mi ha detto di non dire niente.
To transform questions: «Vieni?» → mi ha chiesto se venivo; «Dove sei?» → mi ha chiesto dove ero.

Florence, early June. Matei is in Rome for three days at a restoration conference. Ion and Doina are celebrating forty years of marriage, and Matei is secretly preparing a surprise party in Florence. In the evening he calls Giulia.
Well? Did you talk to my mother? What did she tell you?
She told me she was very happy and that they would arrive on Saturday.
Saturday? But I'd told her Friday! Did she tell you what time?
She told me the train arrived at eight, but that she didn't know if it was morning or evening.
Typical. And my father? Does he know anything about the party?
No. Your mother urged me not to tell him anything. She said that if he found out, he wouldn't come.
And then she asked if Signor Franco would come to the party!
Yes, I translated! She spoke Romanian and a bit of Italian, I spoke a bit of Romanian and lots of Italian.
Oh no. Pietro, what exactly did she tell you about the train?
She said: "Sosim sâmbătă la opt." I understood that sâmbătă meant Saturday.
And it does mean Saturday. Well done. So the mistake is mine. I'd told her the party was on Friday!
"sarebbero arrivati" = would arrive (future in the past)
Four light syllables, stress on the second-to-last, "RI": ri-fe-REE-re.
Stress on "TE", voiced S between vowels: ma-lin-TE-zo.
If the introducing verb is in the PRESENT (dice che…), the tenses don't change. If it is in the PAST (ha detto che…, disse che…), the tenses "take a step back":

In Romanian the tense does NOT change: "A spus că e bucuroasă / că vor sosi". In Italian the change is obligatory: "Ha detto che era contenta / che sarebbero arrivati." (English also shifts tenses, as in "She said she was happy".)
Think of an old photo: the "today" in the photo is no longer your today. That's why it becomes "that day".
Doina ha detto che lei veniva con suo marito.
Matei ha detto a Giulia che la chiamava quella sera.
Ion ha detto che loro erano stanchi.
Always ask yourself: who is speaking now, and about whom? Doina's "io" becomes "lei" when you tell it.
Mi ha detto di non dire niente.
Ci ha chiesto di venire presto.
Useful verbs for reported orders: dire di, chiedere di, pregare di, raccomandare di, ordinare di, consigliare di.
Mi ha chiesto se venivo alla festa.
Mi ha chiesto se avevo già prenotato.
Questions without a question word take "se" (= if, whether). Those with dove, chi, quando, perché keep the word. In careful style the congiuntivo can also be used: "Mi ha chiesto dove fossimo."
She said they would arrive on Saturday.
He said he would come back the next day.
He said he had been tired the day before.
He told me not to say anything.
He asked me if I was coming to the party.
She said it was hot there.
«Questo regalo è per te.» → Ha detto che…

Che cosa aveva detto Matei a sua madre?
Che cosa ha raccomandato Doina a Giulia?
Di non dire niente a Ion
Di chi è l’errore, alla fine?

The idea had come to Matei in May, while he was looking at an old photo of his parents on their wedding day: Ion with a black moustache and his railway uniform, Doina in a white dress sewn by her mother and holding a bunch of wild flowers. It was 14 June forty years earlier, in Sibiu. "Ruby wedding," Graziella had said, looking at the photo over his shoulder. "It must be celebrated. And it must be celebrated here." Matei had tried to object that his parents hated surprises. Graziella had replied that nobody hates surprises, only badly organised ones.

The plan was simple. Doina knew everything, Ion nothing. Doina would tell Ion they were going to Florence to see Viola, and that was all. On Friday 13 June, the evening before the anniversary, there would be a dinner at the trattoria with their Florence friends and a cake with forty candles. The problem was that that very week Matei had to go to Rome for a restorers' conference, from Monday to Thursday. And so the whole organisation went through other people. Which is always the best way to organise a disaster.

The first link in the chain was Pietro. On Monday evening Doina phoned the trattoria to speak to Giulia, but he answered. Doina told him, in a mix of Romanian and Italian, that the train ticket was booked and that they would arrive "sâmbătă la opt". Pietro, who had been hearing Matei speak Romanian on the phone for two years, understood "Saturday at eight" and wrote it on a slip of paper he stuck on the fridge. Then Doina asked him if Matei had ordered the cake, and Pietro said yes, although he had no idea, because it seemed the kindest answer.

The second link was Giulia. When she came back from the workshop, Pietro reported the phone call to her. "She said they would arrive on Saturday at eight and asked me if Matei had ordered the cake. I told her yes." "And has he ordered it?" asked Giulia. "I don't know," admitted Pietro. Giulia called Matei in Rome. Matei said no, he hadn't ordered the cake, and anyway the party was on Friday, not Saturday. "I've told her ten times," he said. "Friday. Vineri. I even sent her a written message."

The third link was Signor Franco, who dropped into the trattoria on Tuesday morning for his coffee. Graziella told him the problem. Franco, who had been a stationmaster for thirty-five years, immediately offered to check the train times. He came back an hour later with a sheet full of numbers. "On Fridays there's a train from Vienna that arrives at Santa Maria Novella at eight in the evening," he announced. "But on Saturdays at eight in the morning there's one from Venice. It depends where they change." Nobody knew where they were changing.

On Wednesday Giulia decided to settle the matter and called Doina directly. But Doina couldn't speak freely, because Ion was in the next room. So she spoke in a whisper, quickly, half in Romanian and half in a very creative Italian. Giulia understood three things: that they were very happy, that Ion suspected nothing, and that the train arrived "at eight". When she asked "morning or evening?", Doina answered something that might have been "evening" or "tomorrow evening", and then hung up abruptly, because Ion was coming in.

That evening Giulia reported the conversation to Matei. "Your mother told me they were very happy and that your father suspected nothing. She told me the train arrived at eight, but I don't know if it's morning or evening. Then she urged me not to tell anyone anything and hung up." "Anyone?" asked Matei. "But half the neighbourhood already knows!" It was true. Graziella had told the baker because of the cake, the baker had told the fruit seller, and the fruit seller, of course, had told the whole Santo Spirito market.

On Thursday evening, when Matei got back from Rome, the trattoria had become an operations centre. On the fridge there were four different slips of paper, written by four different people, with four different times. Pietro's slip said: "Saturday 8 o'clock". Giulia's: "8 o'clock (morning? evening?)". Franco's: "Fri. 20:05 from Vienna / Sat. 8:12 from Venice". And the fruit seller's, which nobody had asked for, said: "Arriving tomorrow, bring strawberries".

Matei looked at them all, then picked up the phone and did what he should have done from the start: he called his father. Not about the party, of course, but with an excuse. "Dad, what time does your train arrive? So I can come and pick you up." Ion answered with the precision of a man who had worked forty years on the railways: "Sâmbătă, ora opt și douăsprezece, de la Veneția. Peronul nu-l știu încă." Saturday, eight twelve, from Venice. He didn't know the platform yet.

Matei hung up and sat down. "They were all right," he said. "Pietro was right: Saturday. Franco was right: eight twelve from Venice. Giulia was right: in the morning. The only one who was wrong was me. I'd told my mother the party was on Friday, but she had bought tickets for Saturday, because the 14th is the real anniversary, and according to her you don't celebrate the day before. It brings bad luck." "She's right," said Graziella. "And now we move the party."

Moving the party meant moving the cake, and the cake meant the baker. Pietro was sent to pass on the message. He came back ten minutes later with a complicated answer: the baker had said the cake would be ready on Saturday at noon, but he had run out of candles, so someone had to go and buy them; he had also asked whether the writing should be in Italian or Romanian, because he didn't know how to write Romanian, and that in any case for forty candles the cake had to be bigger, so it cost more.

"And what did you answer?" asked Matei. "I told him the writing had to be in both languages," said Pietro proudly. "And I dictated the Romanian to him: 'La mulți ani'. He asked me what it meant, and I told him it meant 'happy birthday', but that literally it meant 'to many years'." Matei looked at him with new respect. "And the candles?" "He said that if we brought him forty candles by Saturday morning, he'd put them on himself."

On Saturday morning at eight twelve, on platform seven at Santa Maria Novella, there were Matei, Giulia with Viola in her arms, and Signor Franco with his old stationmaster's signal paddle, which he had kept in a drawer since he retired. "For special occasions," he explained. Ion got off the train first, saw the paddle and burst out laughing. Then he saw Viola, who was stretching out her arms to him shouting "Bunicu!", and he stopped laughing, because his eyes were full of tears.

That afternoon, while Doina and the women of the house were secretly getting the trattoria ready, Signor Franco had the hardest task: keeping Ion away from Via Maggio for four hours. He took him to the station bar, then to the railway museum, then back to the bar. Later Franco reported their conversation to Matei with great satisfaction. Ion had told him that Romanian trains were slower, but the conductors were nicer. He had asked him how many years he had worked in Florence and whether he missed the job. Franco had answered that he missed it every day except Sunday. And at the end Ion had asked him, very seriously, whether by any chance something was being organised behind his back. "And what did you tell him?" asked Matei, worried. "I told him that in Florence nobody ever organises anything," answered Franco. "He believed me at once. You can tell he knows Italians."

The party was that evening, in the trattoria. Ion thought he was going to a family dinner, and instead he found forty people, an enormous cake with the words "Tanti auguri — La mulți ani" and Bellini playing, very badly, an accordion borrowed from the barman. Ion stood in the doorway for a long moment, not understanding. Then he looked at Doina. "Tu știai?" he asked her. Pietro, who was next to him, immediately translated for everyone, out loud, like a real interpreter: "He asked her if she knew!"

Doina answered something in Romanian that made Matei laugh. Everyone turned to Pietro. Pietro hesitated. "She said," he began cautiously, "that she'd known for a month, that it hadn't been easy to keep quiet, and that this was the only surprise she'd managed to give him in forty years." Matei shook his head, laughing. "That's not quite what she said," he specified. "She said it was the only surprise he hadn't discovered in forty years." Ion raised his hands in surrender, and the whole trattoria applauded.

Later Ion made a short speech in Romanian, glass in hand. Matei translated sentence by sentence. Ion said that forty years earlier, on their wedding day, the train to Sibiu had arrived two hours late and Doina had waited in the church thinking he had run away. He said that since then he had never again been late for anything. And he said that on that day, in Florence, he had understood something: that a family is like a railway, made of many distant stations, but all connected.

That night, putting Viola to bed, Matei told her about the evening as if she could understand everything. "Grandpa said it was the most beautiful day of the last forty years. Grandma said Grandpa had said the same thing ten years ago. Bellini said he would stop playing the accordion, and everyone said that was a good idea." Viola, half asleep, opened one eye and said a single, very clear word: "Torta." Matei laughed softly. "Yes," he said. "The cake had its say too."
